title: Internet of Things and Smart Cities
summary: Everyday objects that sense, think and act: how IoT devices use sensors, actuators and the cloud, how smart homes and smart cities work, why they can be risky, and how to design a responsible IoT solution.
learn: What the Internet of Things is and how IoT systems are built
How sensors and actuators work in an input-process-output system
The benefits and risks of smart home devices
How smart cities use data to improve services
Why IoT devices are often insecure, and how the law and users can fix it
How to design an IoT solution responsibly
intro: Doorbells that see, bins that report when they're full, streetlights that dim when nobody's around: billions of everyday objects are now connected to the internet. In this topic you'll find out how the Internet of Things works, explore smart homes and smart cities, discover how hackers can take over badly secured devices, learn about the UK law that banned default passwords, and design your own IoT solution.

pages.title: Things that talk
pages.spec: Explain what the Internet of Things is and describe the parts of an IoT system
pages.summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) is the network of everyday physical objects with sensors, processors and internet connections, so they can collect data, share it and act on it. A typical system has devices, a connection, the cloud and an app.
pages.starter: List everything in your home that is connected to the internet. Which would your grandparents never have imagined online?
sc: I can explain what the Internet of Things is
I can describe the four parts of an IoT system
I can give examples of IoT in different areas of life

b: The Internet of Things (IoT): physical objects connected to the internet
They sense, share data and sometimes act on their own
Doorbells, watches, thermostats, cars, farm sensors, bins, streetlights
There are now well over 15 billion IoT devices worldwide
slides.n: Estimates vary by source; it's in the tens of billions and rising.

b: 1 Device: sensors and/or actuators, plus a small computer (embedded system)
2 Connectivity: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile (4G/5G) or low-power networks
3 Cloud: servers that store and analyse the data
4 App or dashboard: where people see data and control things
Home: smart speakers, thermostats, doorbells, plugs
Health: fitness trackers, glucose monitors
Farming: soil sensors, livestock trackers
Industry and cities: machine monitoring, traffic sensors, smart bins

blocks.text: What is the Internet of Things?

The **[[Internet of Things]]** (IoT) is the huge network of physical objects (not just computers and phones) that have sensors, a small processor and an internet connection. A **[[smart device]]** can collect data about the world, share it, and sometimes act on it automatically. There are now tens of billions of IoT devices in homes, hospitals, farms, factories and city streets.
Parts of an IoT system

blocks.caption: The four parts of an IoT system
head: Part
What it does
Example: a smart thermostat
rows: Senses and/or acts, using a small built-in computer
Measures temperature; switches the boiler on and off
Sends data to and from the device
Stores and analyses data on remote servers
Learns your routine and works out a heating schedule
Lets people see data and send commands
Phone app showing the temperature, with a slider to change it

blocks.text: Most IoT devices contain an **[[embedded system]]**: a small computer built into a larger device to do one specific job. Unlike a laptop, you usually can't install other programs on it.
IoT in different areas

blocks.title: Examples of IoT
items: Home: smart speakers, lights, plugs, doorbells and thermostats
Health: fitness trackers and continuous glucose monitors for people with diabetes
Farming: soil-moisture sensors, livestock collars, automated milking
Industry: sensors that predict when a machine needs repairing
Cities: traffic sensors, smart bins, air-quality monitors

blocks.title: IoT detective
steps: Look at the six product cards (e.g. a smart doorbell, a cattle collar, a bin sensor).
For each, identify its device, connectivity, cloud and app parts.
Decide which one would be most useful in Fermanagh and explain why.

q.q: Describe the four parts of the smart doorbell.
q.a: Device: camera, microphone, motion sensor and button; connectivity: home Wi-Fi; cloud: stores video clips and detects people; app: phone notifications, live video and two-way talk.

q.q: Which device would be most useful in Fermanagh, and why?
q.a: E.g. livestock collars, because farming is a major industry and they can alert farmers to sick or missing animals across large, remote farms.

check.q: What is the Internet of Things?
o: Everyday physical objects connected to the internet

check.q: What is an embedded system?
o: A small computer built into a device to do one job

check.q: What does the cloud do in an IoT system?
o: Stores and analyses data on remote servers

check.q: Which is an example of an IoT device?

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the Internet of Things.
practice.a: Everyday physical objects with sensors/processors (1) connected to the internet so they can share data and act on it (1).

practice.q: Describe the four parts of an IoT system using a fitness tracker as an example.
practice.a: Device: sensors measure heart rate/steps (1); connectivity: Bluetooth to phone/Wi-Fi (1); cloud: stores and analyses activity data (1); app: shows stats/goals (1).

pages.title: Sensors and actuators
pages.spec: Describe common sensors and actuators and how they form an input-process-output system
pages.summary: Sensors measure the physical world and turn it into data (input). A processor follows rules to decide what to do (process). Actuators make something happen in the physical world, such as a motor turning or a light switching on (output). Feedback loops let systems keep conditions steady.
pages.starter: A greenhouse waters its plants automatically when the soil is dry. What does it need to "know" and what does it need to "do"?
sc: I can name common sensors and what they measure
I can name common actuators and what they do
I can describe an IoT system as input, process and output with feedback

b: Sensors measure something about the world and turn it into data
Temperature, light, motion, moisture, sound, distance, air quality, location (GPS)
Many are tiny and cheap
A sensor alone just measures: it needs a processor to decide
Actuators make something happen in the physical world
Motors, pumps, valves, speakers, lights, locks, heaters
Controlled by signals from the processor
Example: open a window when the greenhouse is too hot
Input: sensor reading (soil moisture = 20%)
Process: rule (IF moisture < 30% THEN water)
Output: actuator (pump on for 10 seconds)
Feedback: measure again and repeat, keeping conditions steady

blocks.text: Sensors
A **[[sensor]]** measures something about the physical world and turns it into data a computer can use.

blocks.caption: Common sensors
head: Sensor
Measures
Example use
rows: Streetlights that switch on at dusk
Parking sensors, smart bin fill levels

blocks.text: Actuators

An **[[actuator]]** makes something happen in the physical world, turning a signal from the processor into movement, light, sound or heat. Examples include motors, pumps, valves, speakers, LEDs, electric locks and heaters.
Input, process, output and feedback

blocks.title: An automatic greenhouse
blocks.context: A greenhouse should keep its soil moist.
steps: Input: a moisture sensor reads 22%.
Process: the program checks the rule IF moisture < 30% THEN water.
Output: an actuator (a pump) turns on for 10 seconds.
Feedback: after a minute, the sensor reads again (now 35%), so the pump stays off.
blocks.answer: Measuring again after acting creates a feedback loop that keeps the soil within the right range automatically.

blocks.text: A **[[feedback loop]]** happens when a system's output affects its next input, letting it adjust continuously. Thermostats, cruise control and self-balancing robots all use feedback loops.
If your school has BBC micro:bits, you can build a mini IoT system: the micro:bit has built-in light and temperature sensors, a compass and an accelerometer, and can control LEDs, buzzers and motors.

blocks.title: Design a control system
steps: Choose a problem: a plant that needs watering, a room that gets too hot, or a pet bowl that needs refilling.
Choose the sensor(s) and actuator(s) you need.
Write the rule(s) as IF ... THEN ... statements.
Draw an input-process-output diagram with a feedback arrow.

q.q: Write your sensor, actuator and rules.
q.a: E.g. Room too hot: sensor = temperature; actuators = motorised window opener and fan; rules: IF temperature > 24 °C THEN open window AND fan on; IF temperature < 21 °C THEN close window AND fan off.

q.q: Explain how feedback keeps your system working without a person.
q.a: The sensor keeps measuring after the actuator acts; when conditions return to the target range, the rule switches the actuator off, so the system keeps adjusting itself automatically.

check.q: What does a sensor do?
o: Measures something in the physical world and turns it into data

check.q: What does an actuator do?
o: Makes something happen in the physical world

check.q: Which is an actuator?
What is a feedback loop?
o: When a system's output affects its next input so it can adjust

practice.q: Describe how an automatic streetlight works as an input-process-output system.
practice.a: Input: light sensor measures brightness (1); process: IF light level below a threshold THEN switch on (1); output: actuator/lamp switches on (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a sensor and an actuator.
practice.a: A sensor measures/detects something and sends data in (1); an actuator receives a signal and does something physical, e.g. moves/lights up (1).

pages.title: Smart homes
pages.spec: Evaluate the benefits and risks of smart home devices
pages.summary: Smart home devices can save energy, add convenience and help people live independently, but they also collect personal data, can be hacked, may stop working if the company closes down, and can be misused to watch or control others.
pages.starter: Would you like a home where the lights, heating and locks all respond to your voice? What could go wrong?
sc: I can describe benefits of smart home devices
I can describe privacy and security risks
I can make a reasoned judgement about a smart home device

b: Convenience: control lights, heating and music by voice or app
Energy saving: heating only when needed, smart plugs, smart meters
Independence: reminders and alerts help older or disabled people live at home
Security: cameras and smart locks you can check from anywhere
Privacy: devices collect data about your routines, voice and video
Security: weak devices can be hacked and used to spy or attack
Dependence: if the company's servers shut down, some devices stop working
Misuse: devices can be used to monitor or control people in the home
Interoperability: devices from different brands working together
New standards like Matter aim to make smart home devices compatible
Local control means some things keep working without the internet
Check before you buy: updates, privacy settings, data storage

blocks.text: Smart homes

A **[[smart home]]** has devices that can be controlled remotely or automatically, such as lights, heating, plugs, locks, cameras and speakers. Many are controlled through a **[[voice assistant]]** (like Alexa, Google Assistant or Siri) or a phone app.
Benefits and risks

blocks.caption: Weighing up smart homes
head: Benefits
Risks
rows: Convenience: control things by voice or app
Privacy: data about voices, video and daily routines is collected
Energy saving: smarter heating and lighting
Security: badly secured devices can be hacked
Independence for older and disabled people
Dependence on a company: devices may stop working if it closes
Peace of mind: check cameras and locks remotely
Misuse: devices can be used to watch or control someone else

blocks.text: **[[privacy|Privacy]]** is a major concern. A smart speaker listens for its "wake word"; cameras may record your home; thermostats know when you're out. This data is often sent to company servers and may be used for advertising or shared with others.

Smart home devices can be misused to monitor or control people in a household. If someone uses technology to track or frighten you, tell a trusted adult. Organisations such as Women's Aid offer help with technology misuse.
Interoperability

**[[interoperability]]** means devices from different makers working together. For years, smart home devices often only worked with their own brand's app. New standards such as **Matter** aim to let devices from different brands work together, and some allow local control, so they keep working even if the internet goes down.

blocks.title: Before buying a smart device, check
items: Does the company promise security updates, and for how long?
What data does it collect, where is it stored and who can see it?
Can you change privacy settings and delete your data?
Will it still work if the internet goes down or the company closes?

blocks.title: Smart home audit
steps: Your teacher gives you the privacy policies (simplified) for three smart devices: a speaker, a doorbell camera and a thermostat.
For each, record what data it collects, where it goes and how long it's kept.
Score each device out of 5 for privacy and explain your score.
Write advice for a family deciding whether to buy one.

q.q: Which device scored lowest for privacy, and why?
q.a: Usually the doorbell camera: it records video of visitors and passers-by, stores clips in the cloud for a long time, and may share data with others.

q.q: Write your advice to the family.
q.a: E.g. "Buy the thermostat: it saves energy and collects little personal data. If you buy the doorbell, turn off cloud recording you don't need, set a strong password with two-factor authentication, and point it so it doesn't record the street or neighbours."

check.q: Which is a benefit of smart home devices?
o: Saving energy by heating only when needed

check.q: Which is a privacy risk of smart speakers?
o: They may record and send voice data to company servers

check.q: What is interoperability?
o: Operating a device with your voice
Devices from different makers working together

check.q: Why might a smart device stop working one day?
o: The Wi-Fi password is too long
The company might shut down its servers

practice.q: Describe one benefit and one risk of using a smart doorbell.
practice.a: Benefit: see who's at the door remotely/security/deliveries (1); risk: privacy of visitors/hacking/cloud storage of video (1).

practice.q: Evaluate whether an older person living alone should have smart home devices.
practice.a: Benefits, e.g. reminders, alerts if they fall, voice control helps independence (1-2); risks, e.g. privacy, complexity, scams/hacking, cost (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: Smart cities
pages.spec: Describe how smart cities use IoT data to improve services, and discuss the concerns
pages.summary: Smart cities use sensors and data to manage traffic, energy, waste, air quality and public services more efficiently. They can save money and reduce pollution but raise concerns about surveillance, cost, who owns the data, and who is left out.
pages.starter: Your town has 500 bins. Some fill up in a day, others take a week. How could a council empty them more efficiently?
sc: I can describe examples of smart city technology
I can explain how data helps cities make decisions
I can discuss concerns about smart cities

b: A smart city uses sensors and data to run services better
Traffic lights that adapt to queues
Bins that report when they're full, so lorries only collect full ones
Streetlights that dim when nobody's around
Air-quality sensors show where pollution is worst
Real-time bus tracking on apps and stops
Smart parking: find a free space without circling
Digital twins: virtual copies of a city to test changes before building them
Surveillance: cameras and sensors everywhere can track people
Who owns and controls the data: the council or private companies?
Cost, maintenance and hacking risks
Will everyone benefit, or only people with smartphones?

blocks.text: What is a smart city?
A **[[smart city]]** uses IoT sensors, networks and data analysis to manage services such as transport, energy, waste and public safety more efficiently and sustainably.

blocks.caption: Smart city examples
head: Service
Smart solution
Benefit
rows: Lorries only collect full bins, saving fuel and time
LED streetlights that dim or brighten with movement
Saves energy; lights where people are
Traffic lights that adapt to queues
Passengers know when the bus will arrive
Shows where pollution is worst so action can be targeted

blocks.text: Data and decisions

Smart cities collect enormous amounts of data. Many publish some of it as **[[open data]]** so researchers, businesses and citizens can use it to create apps and spot problems. Some cities build a **[[digital twin]]**: a detailed virtual model of the city, updated with live data, where planners can test changes (like a new road or flood defence) before spending money in the real world.
Belfast has a Smart Belfast programme that has tested ideas such as sensors to monitor air quality and footfall. You can find Northern Ireland datasets on OpenDataNI.
Concerns

blocks.title: Questions to ask about smart cities
items: **[[surveillance|Surveillance]]**: are cameras and sensors tracking individual people?
Data ownership: who owns the data, and is it shared with private companies?
Security: what happens if city systems are hacked?
Cost: who pays for installing and maintaining sensors?
Fairness: do services still work for people without smartphones?

blocks.title: Smart Enniskillen
steps: Your group is the council's smart town team for Enniskillen (or your own town).
Choose two problems to solve (e.g. traffic on the bridges, flooding from the lough, litter, tourist parking).
For each, describe the sensors, data and actions your smart solution would use.
Complete a concerns checklist for each solution and present your plan.

q.q: Describe one smart solution: sensors, data and actions.
q.a: E.g. Flooding: water-level sensors on the lough and rivers send live data to the council; when levels pass a threshold, the system alerts residents by text and triggers road-closure signs.

q.q: What is the biggest concern about your plan and how would you address it?
q.a: E.g. "Cameras for traffic counting could identify people, so we'd use sensors that only count vehicles, delete images immediately and publish the rules."

check.q: What is a smart city?
o: A city that uses sensors and data to run services better
A city with lots of phone shops

check.q: How do smart bins save money?
o: Lorries only collect bins that are full

check.q: What is a digital twin?
o: A virtual model of a real place, updated with live data

check.q: Which is a concern about smart cities?

practice.q: Describe how sensors could be used to reduce traffic congestion in a town.
practice.a: Sensors detect queues/vehicle numbers (1); data is processed to adjust traffic lights/timings (1); drivers informed of delays/alternative routes, reducing congestion (1).

practice.q: "Every town should become a smart city." Discuss.
practice.a: Benefits, e.g. efficiency, less pollution, better services (1-2); concerns, e.g. surveillance, cost, hacking, digital divide (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: Hacking the things
pages.spec: Explain why IoT devices are often insecure and describe how laws and users can make them safer
pages.summary: Many IoT devices have been sold with weak default passwords and no updates, so attackers can take them over in large numbers to form botnets. UK law now bans universal default passwords on new smart devices, and users can protect themselves with good habits.
pages.starter: A webcam is sold with the username "admin" and password "admin". Why is that a problem when millions are sold?
sc: I can explain why IoT devices are often insecure
I can describe a botnet attack
I can describe the UK's PSTI rules and good security habits

slides.t: Why IoT is easy to attack
b: Many devices shipped with the same default password, like admin/admin
Cheap devices often never get security updates
Owners forget they're connected and never change settings
Each device is a computer that attackers can control
A botnet is a network of hijacked devices controlled by criminals
In 2016 the Mirai botnet took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers
It used them to flood an internet company with traffic, taking major websites offline
Owners usually have no idea their device is involved
The UK PSTI rules (from April 2024) ban universal default passwords on new smart devices
Makers must say how long they'll provide security updates
Makers must give a way to report security problems
You: change passwords, update firmware, use a separate guest network

blocks.text: Why are IoT devices insecure?
Many IoT devices are cheap, simple and rushed to market. Common problems include:

items: **[[default password|Default passwords]]** like "admin" that are the same on every device and published online
No security updates: the **[[firmware]]** (the software built into the device) is never fixed
Owners don't realise the device is a computer that needs protecting
Weak encryption, or data sent without encryption

blocks.text: Botnets

A **[[botnet]]** is a network of devices infected with malware and controlled by criminals without their owners knowing. In 2016, the **Mirai** botnet scanned the internet for devices using default usernames and passwords. It took over hundreds of thousands of webcams, video recorders and routers, then used them to flood an internet company with traffic in a "distributed denial of service" (DDoS) attack, which took major websites offline across parts of the US and Europe.
The law: PSTI
Since April 2024, the UK's **[[PSTI]]** rules (from the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act) require makers of new consumer smart devices sold in the UK to:

items: Ban universal default passwords: each device needs a unique password, or the user must set one.
Tell customers how long the device will receive security updates.
Provide a way for people to report security problems.

blocks.text: The UK was one of the first countries in the world to make these rules law.
Protecting your devices

blocks.title: IoT security habits
items: Change any default password to a strong, unique one
Turn on automatic updates; check for firmware updates
Use two-factor authentication on the app account
Put smart devices on a separate guest network if your router allows
Turn off features you don't use (e.g. remote access)
Before buying, check how long it will receive updates

blocks.title: Secure the smart home
steps: Read the description of the Murphy family's smart home: 8 devices, some old, some with default passwords, all on the main Wi-Fi.
Find at least five security problems.
Write an action plan, putting the fixes in priority order.
Explain which problem the PSTI law would have prevented.

q.q: List the five problems you found.
q.a: E.g. camera still uses admin/admin; doorbell firmware not updated for 2 years; all devices on the same network as laptops; app account has no two-factor authentication; old plug no longer gets updates.

q.q: Write your top three fixes and explain the order.
q.a: 1 Change default passwords (easiest for attackers to exploit); 2 update firmware and replace devices that no longer get updates; 3 move devices to a guest network and turn on two-factor authentication.

check.q: Why are default passwords dangerous?
o: They're the same on many devices and often published online

check.q: What is a botnet?
o: A network of robots in a factory
A network of hijacked devices controlled by criminals

check.q: What did the Mirai botnet do in 2016?
o: Took over IoT devices with default passwords and attacked an internet company

check.q: Since 2024, what do the UK PSTI rules ban?
o: Universal default passwords on new smart devices
check.why: Each device needs a unique password.

practice.q: Explain why IoT devices are often less secure than laptops or phones.
practice.a: Any three: default/weak passwords (1); few or no security updates (1); owners don't realise they need securing (1); cheap/rushed design/weak encryption (1).

practice.q: Describe two things the UK PSTI rules require from smart device manufacturers.
practice.a: Any two: no universal default passwords (1); state how long security updates will be provided (1); provide a way to report vulnerabilities (1).

pages.title: Design an IoT solution
pages.spec: Design an IoT solution to a real problem, considering users, data, security and sustainability
pages.summary: Good IoT design starts with a real problem and real users, then plans the sensors, actuators, connectivity and data, and builds in security, privacy and sustainability from the start, a principle called "by design".
pages.starter: Name one problem at school or in your town that a connected sensor could help with.
sc: I can define a problem and its users
I can plan the hardware, data and rules for an IoT system
I can apply security, privacy and sustainability by design

b: Who has the problem, and what do they actually need?
Would a non-tech solution be simpler?
What would success look like?
User stories: "As a ..., I want ..., so that ..."
Sensors: what needs measuring?
Actuators and alerts: what should happen?
Connectivity and power: Wi-Fi, mobile or low-power network? Battery or mains?
Data: what's collected, how often, where it goes, who sees it
Security by design: unique passwords, encryption, updates
Privacy by design: collect only what's needed; no cameras if a sensor will do
Sustainability: low power, long-lasting, repairable, recyclable
Make a prototype and test it with real users

blocks.text: From problem to plan

Good IoT design starts with a real problem and real users, not with a gadget. Ask who has the problem, what they need, and whether technology is even the right answer. A **user story** helps: "As a school caretaker, I want to know which classrooms have windows open after school, so that I can save heating and keep the building secure."

blocks.caption: IoT design plan
head: Part
Questions to answer
rows: Who needs this? What does success look like?
What must be measured, and where?
What happens automatically? Who gets told?
Wi-Fi, mobile or low-power network? Battery or mains power?
What's collected, how often, where is it stored, who can see it?
What IF ... THEN ... decisions does the system make?

blocks.text: "By design"
Designers now try to build good qualities in from the very start, rather than adding them later:

items: **Security by design**: unique passwords, encrypted data, regular updates.
**[[privacy by design]]**: collect only the data you really need. For example, use a simple motion counter rather than a camera.
**[[sustainability]]**: low power use, long battery life, repairable and recyclable parts, and a long working life.

blocks.text: Prototype and test

A **[[prototype]]** is an early working model used to test ideas. With a micro:bit or similar board, you can prototype an IoT system with real sensors in a lesson, test it with users and improve it before anything expensive is built.

blocks.title: IoT design challenge
steps: Choose a problem at school or in your town (e.g. classroom windows left open, a car park that's always full, a school garden that dries out).
Write a user story and complete the IoT design plan table.
Write at least three IF ... THEN ... rules.
Add a "by design" box for security, privacy and sustainability. If you have micro:bits, prototype one part.

q.q: Write your user story and your three rules.
q.a: E.g. "As the eco-club leader, I want the garden watered when it's dry so that plants survive the holidays." Rules: IF soil moisture < 30% AND it isn't raining THEN pump on for 20 s; IF water tank < 10% THEN send alert; IF temperature < 2 °C THEN don't water.

q.q: Describe how your design is secure, private and sustainable.
q.a: E.g. secure: unique password and encrypted connection; private: only soil data, no cameras; sustainable: solar-powered battery, waterproof case for a long life, recyclable parts.

check.q: What should IoT design start with?
o: A real problem and the users who have it

check.q: What is privacy by design?
o: Building privacy in from the start, collecting only the data needed
Adding a privacy policy at the end

check.q: What is a prototype?
o: An early working model used to test ideas

check.q: Which choice makes an IoT design more sustainable?
o: Low power use and repairable parts
check.why: Sustainability means a long, low-impact life.

practice.q: Explain how privacy by design could be applied to a system that counts people using a library.
practice.a: Use a simple counter/motion sensor instead of a camera (1); don't store personal data/identities (1); store only totals and delete raw data/limit access (1).

practice.q: Give two questions a designer should ask about data in an IoT system.
practice.a: Any two: what data is collected (1); how often (1); where it's stored (1); who can see it (1); how long it's kept (1).

glossary.def: The network of everyday physical objects that have sensors, processors and internet connections.
An everyday object that can collect data, connect to the internet and sometimes act automatically.
Remote servers, reached over the internet, that store and process data.
A small computer built into a larger device to carry out one specific job.
A device that measures something in the physical world and turns it into data.
A device that makes something happen in the physical world, such as a motor, pump or light.
When a system's output affects its next input, letting it adjust automatically.
A home with devices that can be controlled remotely or automatically.
Software that responds to spoken commands, such as Alexa, Google Assistant or Siri.
Having control over your personal information and who can see it.
The ability of devices or systems from different makers to work together.
A city that uses sensors, networks and data to run services more efficiently.
Data that anyone is allowed to use for free.
Watching or tracking people, for example with cameras or sensors.
A virtual model of a real place or object, kept updated with live data.
The password a device comes with from the factory.
A network of devices infected with malware and controlled by criminals.
The software built into a device that controls how it works.
The UK's Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure rules, which set minimum security requirements for smart devices.
An early working model used to test and improve an idea.
Building privacy into a system from the start, for example by collecting only the data needed.
Meeting today's needs without harming the environment or future generations.
